q.q: What is a game platform?
o: The style or category a game belongs to
The device or system a game runs on
The software used to design and build a game
The group of people a game is aimed at
q.why: A game platform is the device a game is played on, e.g. console, mobile phone or computer; a category is a genre.

q.q: Which of these is a game platform?
q.why: Consoles, mobile phones and computers are platforms; sprites, genres and leader boards are parts or types of games.

q.q: How has gaming changed over the generations of platforms?
o: From discs and single player to downloads, cloud and online multiplayer
From mobile phones back to large coin-operated arcade machines
From online multiplayer back to installing games from discs
From downloads and the cloud back to punched cards and tape
q.why: Gaming moved from installing discs and playing alone to downloading, cloud technology and online multiplayer.

q.q: How do leader boards help in an educational game?
o: They stop players from skipping levels
They let players take on different roles
They make the game load more quickly
They motivate players to improve their scores
q.why: Climbing above classmates on a leader board is motivating.

q.q: In an educational game, why can you not move to the next level before completing the one before?
o: So the game does not run out of memory
So players can take on a new role
So skills are built step by step
So the leader board is updated correctly
q.why: Rules and levels of increasing difficulty build skills gradually.

q.q: How do roles in an educational game deepen learning?
o: Players see their score compared with classmates
Players can skip levels they find too hard
Players are given more lives for each role
Players reflect on what happened in certain situations
q.why: Taking on different roles lets you reflect on situations; comparing scores is the leader board.

q.q: A game always tells you to collect the key to reach the next level. Which feature of a good game is this?
q.why: A clear aim means you know what you are trying to do.

q.q: A game has secret areas and a high score table that make people want to play it again. Which feature is this?
q.why: High scores, secrets and multiplayer give replay value.

q.q: A game starts easy and gets harder gradually, but is never impossible. Which feature of a good game does this show?
q.why: The right level of challenge is not too easy, not impossible, and gets harder gradually.

q.q: In a game for young children, the graphics, sound and story all fit together. Which feature is this?
q.why: A consistent theme means graphics, sound and story fit together and suit the audience.

q.q: When does the history of video games begin?
q.why: Academic computer scientists began designing simple games in the early 1950s.

q.q: How were programs and moves often fed into early university computers?
q.why: Punched cards had holes that the computer could read.

q.q: When did video gaming become popular with the general public?
q.why: Arcades, home consoles and home computer games made gaming mainstream in the 1970s and 1980s.

q.q: Which game is most often named as the first video game made purely for fun?
q.why: Tennis for Two (1958) is usually called the first video game made purely for entertainment.

q.q: Who created Tennis for Two?
q.why: Physicist William Higinbotham created it; technician Robert Dvorak built it.

q.q: Why was Tennis for Two created?
o: As part of a PhD on human–computer interaction
To show off the first home games console
To entertain visitors at a laboratory open day
To sell to the public in toy shops
q.why: It was made to show visitors science could be fun; OXO was the PhD project.

q.q: How did players control Tennis for Two?
o: A knob to set the angle and a button to hit
A keyboard and punched cards to enter moves
A rotary telephone dial to choose a square
A joystick to move and a trigger to hit
q.why: Each controller box had a knob and a button; OXO used a telephone dial.

q.q: What did Tennis for Two use as its screen?
q.why: It showed a side view of a tennis court on a small round oscilloscope screen.

q.q: How was the score kept in Tennis for Two?
o: It was shown in the corner of the screen
It was stored on punched cards
It was printed out at the end of each game
q.why: There was no score on screen; players kept score themselves.

q.q: Which early game was noughts and crosses against the computer on EDSAC?
q.why: OXO (1952) was written by Sandy Douglas at Cambridge University.

q.q: Which game was the first big commercial hit, helping to start the games industry?
q.why: Atari's Pong (1972) was the first big commercial hit.

q.q: Which statement about the very first video games is true?
o: They were experiments, research projects or demonstrations
They were played mainly on home games consoles
They were made to sell in arcades and toy shops
They were all made by Atari during the 1950s
q.why: None of the first games were made to sell; money came later with arcades and consoles.

q.q: Some old slides describe an 'IBM 1560' from 12 August 1981. What machine do those details really describe?
o: The analogue computer used for Tennis for Two
q.why: The details describe the IBM PC 5150, a 1980s home and office PC, not a 1960s university machine.

q.q: What is GameMaker?
o: A game genre based on building things
A game engine for designing and building 2D games
A game platform such as a console or phone
q.why: GameMaker is a 2D game engine that uses drag-and-drop actions.

q.q: What does it mean that GameMaker uses 'drag and drop'?
o: You build games by dragging action blocks instead of typing code
Games made in it can only be played using a touch screen
You drag finished games in from the internet to edit them
You must type all of the code behind every feature yourself
q.why: Actions are dragged into place, so you can make a game without writing the code yourself.

q.q: What is a sprite?
o: A sound that plays when something happens
Something in the game that can do something
A level or screen where objects are placed
An image that represents something in the game
q.why: Sprites are the pictures; rooms are levels and objects are things that act.

q.q: An animated sprite has...
q.why: Animated sprites have several sub-images shown one after another, like a flip-book.

q.q: A tree in an RPG never moves. How many images does its sprite need?
q.why: A sprite that is not animated is one picture.

q.q: Which is the best name for the enemy's sprite?
q.why: The naming convention uses the prefix spr for sprites; obj is for objects and rm for rooms.

q.q: Why use a naming convention such as spr and obj?
o: So that the order of the rooms is set automatically
So that a sprite is not stretched when it is scaled
So that GameMaker can run the finished game more quickly
So resources like sprPlayer and objPlayer are easy to tell apart
q.why: A prefix says what type of resource it is.

q.q: What size are new sprites in school by default?
q.why: Leave the width and height at 32 pixels.

q.q: Which GameMaker resource holds the scenery behind the action?
q.why: Backgrounds are the scenery; rooms are where objects are placed.

q.q: Which GameMaker resource is described as 'things in the game that can do something'?
q.why: Objects can do things and use sprites to be seen.

q.q: Why must a sprite be made into an object?
o: So it can be given a naming convention
So it can be seen, moved and interact in the game
So it can be scaled to 80%
So it can be saved as a picture file
q.why: An object can be moved, act on other things and be seen.

q.q: What is an instance?
o: A template that uses a sprite
Something that happens, like a key press
A copy of an object placed in a room
q.why: The object is the template; an instance is a placed copy.

q.q: In the cookie cutter comparison, what is the cookie cutter?
q.why: The cutter is the object and each cookie is an instance.

q.q: A maze is built from 100 identical walls. How many wall objects are needed?
q.why: One wall object can be placed as 100 instances.

q.q: Which statement about objects is true?
o: An object can only have one event
Some objects have no sprite and are invisible
Objects are placed directly into the game
Every object must have exactly one sprite
q.why: Some objects are invisible and just control the game.

q.q: A key press or a collision is an example of...
q.why: Events are things that happen in the game.

q.q: Move Fixed is an example of...
q.why: Actions are what the object does when an event happens.

q.q: When does a collision event run?
o: When the game moves to the next room
When an instance is first created
q.why: A collision event runs when two instances touch.

q.q: To make the player move left, which event and action are used?
o: Keyboard Left event with Move Fixed stop, speed 0
Collision event with Move Fixed left, speed 5
Create event with Move Fixed left, speed 5
Keyboard Left event with Move Fixed left, speed 5
q.why: The Keyboard Left event triggers Move Fixed to the left at speed 5.

q.q: The player keeps moving after the arrow key is released. What is the fix?
o: Add the Keyboard 'no key' event with Move Fixed stop, speed 0
Untick Solid on the player object so it can slow down
Add a Create event with Move Fixed in all directions, speed 5
Add a Collision event with objKey that restarts the room
q.why: The no-key event runs when no key is pressed; the centre square with speed 0 stops the player.

q.q: In objWall's collision with objPlayer, why is Move Fixed applied to the Other object?
o: So the player stops, not the wall
So the next room is loaded
So the wall moves out of the way
q.why: Other is the player, so the player is stopped when it hits the wall.

q.q: The player won't fit through a gap in the maze. What do the notes suggest?
o: Scale the sprite to 80% both horizontally and vertically
Scale the sprite to 80% horizontally only, not vertically
Increase the player's speed to 10 so it squeezes through
Untick Solid on every one of the wall objects in the maze
q.why: Scaling both directions keeps the shape; one direction would stretch or squash it.

q.q: Why should Horizontal and Vertical both be ticked when scaling a sprite?
o: So that the sprite becomes solid
So the sprite is not stretched or squashed
So that the sprite is animated
So that the sprite moves faster
q.why: Scaling only one direction squashes the sprite.

q.q: What is a room in GameMaker?
o: A copy of an object in the game
The area where you place your objects
A template that uses a sprite
q.why: A room is where instances of objects are placed.

q.q: What is the minimum number of rooms a game needs to run?
q.why: You must have at least one room.

q.q: Besides levels, which of these would a game normally use rooms for?
o: Title screen, help pages and end credits
q.why: Rooms are used for each level and for opening, help and end screens.

q.q: Why should rooms be aesthetically pleasing?
o: It makes players want to play the game
It is needed for Next Room to work
It makes the game load faster
q.why: Aesthetically pleasing means attractive to look at, which attracts players.

q.q: When first tested, the player runs straight over the key. Why?
o: The key sprite is too small
The key was not given a name
No event tells the key what to do
q.why: Without a collision event, nothing happens when they touch.

q.q: Which event and action make collecting the key move the player on?
o: Collision with objWall, then Restart Game
Collision with objPlayer, then Next Room
q.why: In objKey, a collision with objPlayer triggers the Next Room action.

q.q: Why did the game show a FATAL ERROR when the key was collected?
o: There was no next room to go to
q.why: Next Room needs another room after the current one.

q.q: Why does the finishGame object appear as a ? in the room editor?
o: It is hidden behind a wall
It has an error in its events
It has not been named correctly
q.why: Objects with no sprite have no image to show, so they appear as ?.

q.q: Where must the YouWin room be placed in the list of rooms?
q.why: Rooms run in list order, so the win screen must come last.

q.q: A pupil adds a new level after YouWin in the room list. What will happen?
o: The new level will be played first
GameMaker will move it to the right place
Players will win before playing the new level
The game will skip the YouWin room
q.why: Rooms run in order, so new levels must go between the practice room and YouWin.

q.q: What does ticking Relative do when setting the score to 10?
q.why: Relative changes the current value by that amount.

q.q: Which event makes the enemy start moving when the game begins?
q.why: The Create event runs when the instance first appears.

q.q: Move Fixed has up, down, left and right all selected. What does GameMaker do?
o: Moves in all four directions at once
Stays still because the arrows cancel out
Picks one of those directions at random
Moves up first, then down, then left, then right
q.why: With several directions selected, GameMaker picks one at random.

q.q: Why does objEnemy have a Collision with objWall event using Move Fixed?
o: So that it takes one life away from the player
So that it is destroyed as soon as it touches a wall
So it heads off in a new direction when it hits a wall
So that the game moves on to the next room
q.why: Move Fixed with four directions sends it off a new way.

q.q: What does Set Lives −1 with Relative ticked do?
q.why: Relative changes the current value by −1.

q.q: A player has 3 lives and Set Lives −1 is used without Relative ticked. What will the lives become?
q.why: Without Relative, the value is set to exactly −1 rather than reduced by 1.

q.q: Test Lives with value 0 and operation 'equal to' is an example of...
q.why: It checks whether lives = 0, like an IF in programming.

q.q: What are Start Block and End Block used for?
o: Starting and stopping the background music
Setting the player's first and last life
Marking the first and last room in the game
Grouping the actions that run if the condition is true
q.why: They group the actions belonging to the IF, like brackets in code.

q.q: When the enemy hits the player and Test Lives is TRUE, what happens?
o: The high score table is shown and the game restarts
The game moves to the next room
The player keeps playing with one less life
q.why: Lives = 0 runs the actions between Start Block and End Block.

q.q: When Test Lives is FALSE (lives greater than 0), which actions run?
o: The actions between Start Block and End Block
No actions at all, and the game freezes
q.why: If the condition is false the block is skipped and the actions after Else run.

q.q: Which object sets lives to 3 and shows the score and lives in the caption?
q.why: SetScore has no sprite; in its Create event it shows score and lives and sets lives to 3.

q.q: In the enemy's collision with objPlayer, why does Destroy the Instance come first?
o: So the player is removed from the room
So the lives are set back to 3
So the enemy disappears after hitting the player
So the high score table is cleared
q.why: Destroy the Instance makes the enemy disappear.

q.q: What are the two main types of game sound?
q.why: Game audio has background music, which sets the mood, and SFX, which play when something happens.

q.q: Which is an example of a sound effect rather than background music?
o: A chime when a coin is collected
A theme that plays on the title screen
A song that loops during the credits
A tune that plays throughout level 2
q.why: SFX play when something happens; music plays throughout.

q.q: How can sounds help the player without them having to read anything?
o: They show the player exactly where the walls are
They replace the need for any score at all
They make the game load and run faster
They tell the player whether they are playing successfully
q.why: Sounds give feedback, e.g. a hand-clap celebrating a completed level.

q.q: A game for young children uses a very dark, gloomy background. What is the problem?
o: Dark backgrounds make a game seem scary, so it does not suit the audience
Dark backgrounds make the game file far too large to download
Dark backgrounds stop collision events from working properly
Dark backgrounds cannot be used in GameMaker games at all
q.why: Bright, light backgrounds are more child-friendly; a dark one feels scary.

q.q: Why should the background match the game's genre?
o: Mismatched elements make the game feel clunky and unsuitable for its audience
GameMaker will refuse to run a game with a mismatched background
A matching background makes all of the sprite files smaller
Mismatched backgrounds make the game run much more slowly
q.why: Consistency suits the target audience.

q.q: How are games usually grouped into genres?
o: By the platform it runs on
By what the game is about
By how much the game costs
By their challenges, story and gameplay
q.why: Games are grouped by challenges and gameplay, not content.

q.q: Which genre relies most on hand–eye coordination?
q.why: Action games are physical challenges needing motor skill.

q.q: A puzzle game where you talk to characters and explore without fighting is...
q.why: Adventure games involve solving puzzles without reflex or action challenges.

q.q: Platform and fighting games are subgenres of which genre?
q.why: Platform (Super Mario Bros.) and fighting (Street Fighter) are action subgenres.

q.q: Which game is an example of a role playing game (RPG)?
q.why: In Pokémon your team gains skills while following a storyline through an overworld.

q.q: Which genre needs careful, skilful thinking and planning to win?
q.why: Strategy games, such as Civilization and chess, rely on planning.

q.q: Microsoft Flight Simulator and Farming Simulator belong to which genre?
q.why: Simulation games closely simulate parts of a real or fictional reality.

q.q: Which way of paying lets you play a selection of console games each month?
o: Buying a disc in a shop
q.why: Console games can be bought on disc, downloaded or played through a monthly subscription.

q.q: Where are mobile games usually bought or downloaded?
o: From the app stores on phones and tablets
From discs bought in a shop
q.why: Mobile games are bought or downloaded free from app stores.

q.q: What does VR stand for?
q.why: VR is a computer-created world you experience with a headset.

q.q: What does AR stand for?
q.why: AR adds to (augments) the real world.

q.q: Which technology needs a headset that shows a 360° computer-generated world?
q.why: A VR headset replaces your view with a computer-made 3D world.

q.q: In VR, what happens to the view when you turn your head?
o: It pauses the game until you face forward
It changes to show a different part of the 3D world
It switches to the phone's camera view
It stays the same so you do not feel sick
q.why: The headset shows a 360° view that changes as you turn your head.

q.q: A furniture app shows how a sofa would look in your own living room. This is an example of...
q.why: Computer images are added on top of the real world.

q.q: Which features of a phone does Pokémon Go use?
q.why: GPS places creatures at real locations and the camera shows them.

q.q: Which is a well-known VR game?
q.why: Beat Saber is played on VR headsets; Pokémon Go is AR.

q.q: Why is Minecraft not a true example of a VR game?
o: It has never had a VR version
It uses the phone's camera and GPS
It is a 2D game made in GameMaker
It is normally played on an ordinary screen
q.why: Minecraft has had VR versions but is usually played on a normal screen.

q.q: How many times had Pokémon Go been downloaded by the end of 2016?
q.why: It passed 500 million downloads in 2016; 300 million is Minecraft's sales figure.

q.q: What does 'scoring' refer to in a game?
o: The sketches made of each screen before building
The group of people that the game is aimed at
The number of levels that a game contains
An abstract quantity, usually points, linked to a player or team
q.why: Scoring is usually points; events can raise or lower it.

q.q: Which game uses a 'last man standing' approach instead of a high score table?
q.why: Fortnite and Apex Legends use last man standing.

q.q: Which is an example of a game with no score that you can still win?
q.why: In Solitaire you win by clearing the cards.

q.q: What is a target audience?
o: The people who design and build the game
The score a player needs to win
The particular group of people a product is aimed at
The genre the game belongs to
q.why: The target audience is the intended players.

q.q: Which game is aimed mainly at logical thinkers and often an older generation of gamer?
q.why: The notes give Chess as aimed at logical thinkers; Fortnite is aimed at young teens.

q.q: The Magic Amusements game must be aimed at which target audience?
q.why: The brief asks for a 2D game for ages 10–14.

q.q: Which of these is NOT required by the Magic Amusements brief?
q.why: The brief is for a 2D GameMaker game; 3D is what the company already makes.

q.q: What should each screen of a storyboard be labelled with?
o: The program code for each event
q.why: A storyboard plans each screen's look.

q.q: What usually happens if you build a game straight away without a storyboard?
o: A messy game with no consistent theme
A game with more levels than planned
A game that runs much faster
A game that cannot be saved
q.why: Planning keeps the theme consistent.
